speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it does not matter very much. I must say that the hon. member who rose is not the one I meant; I had in mind an hon. member who has been sitting here for over 12 years, yet nobody seems to know which constituency he represents, because of his stolid silence, his carelessness and the incapacity he has demonstrated since he came to the house.
Mr. Speaker, we are here to discuss an important problem and try to find a solution. If the Postmaster General would condescend to call to order that bunch of unruly members, I believe that the debate would prove more constructive than the one in which some are trying to involve me.

[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
We are now faced with a crucial problem, otherwise this debate would not be taking place this evening. This is a serious problem to the extent that if in the near future, the entire postal system is disrupted on account of the slowdown or the work-to-rule now carried on in Montreal, we might be confronted with a national dispute.
Basically, it is not a simple problem, but the minister does not seem to understand anything. It is a conflict in which 450 union members are threatened to lose their job in a couple of months, but this does not seem to concern the Liberal members from Montreal.
In fact, the employees are only asking that the government take measures to ensure that the tenderers or sub-contractors, whatever they are called, recognize the only bargaining unit which represents them. Since only one contractor provided the postal service in Montreal and the area until now, the minister, in his doubtful wisdom, decided to distribute the postal service among five or six separate contracts.
The employees are threatened because their bargaining unit will not be recognized by the contractors. If this happens, they will no longer have any job security.
Those people are also threatened with losing their seniority. Some employees have held their jobs for over 20 years but with a single stroke of the pen the minister recently threatened their security.
Have we reached the point in this society the Prime Minister calls just, where people are no longer entitled to survival? Ail those employees ask is for the Postmaster General to assure them that they will not be laid off in a month.
Mr. Speaker, I fail to see why the minister did not take a clearer stand in that conflict. He could have benefitted from past experience. We remember the strike that broke out when the mail was delivered by Rod Service Ltd, which also knew of the experience of the former contractor, a certain Senecal whose contract was transferred merely by verbal agreement between the minister and the G. Lapalme Inc. to a new contractor who was forced to respect those contracts, that bargaining unit.
Thanks to that bargaining unit, for which they paid dearly through four years of work and efforts, the employees managed to obtain decent salaries, normal fringe benefits and
February 18, 1970

finally, security of employment, as long as they could work.
Mr. Speaker, the minister has done nothing. He merely said: I am not an employer; I cannot intervene in the conflict since, as minister, it does not behove me to deal with the employees. To my mind, the minister is merely bringing out the hypocrisy inherent in this supposedly just society.
Mr. Speaker, the minister could intervene and he still can do it if he wants, since in the contracts he grants, he himself determines the working conditions such as the minimum wages paid to the people working for the new contractors. And, when the minister is forced to protect the employees and union members by setting up a bargaining unit, he refuses to commit himself and he tries, by devious means, to beg off and to shun his responsibilities.
If the minister needs additional arguments we might be able to oblige him. When he says that he cannot provide a bargaining unit for many employers, I think that he could refer to the Canadian Labour Code. The minister does not know it because he has never been close to the workers but has always represented higher interests. I am not blaming him for it, it is his privilege. But in the House it is his responsiblity, as a minister, to deal with workers and union members. The minister should know about the mechanisms capable of preventing such conflicts.
The minister could resort to the Canadian Labour Code, which permits but one bargaining unit among a group of employers. Besides, this is done in the Montreal area, in the province of Quebec. In fact, there are bargaining units on building sites and the members of all the trade associations have to go from one place to another and belong to a single bargaining unit. And those units have to deal with numerous contractors.
Mr. Speaker, the minister is too ready to find an excuse for his inaction. He could intervene but he refuses to do so and that is why the union members accuse him of wanting to destroy the bargaining unit. I do not accuse him myself, but I wonder whether his refusal to reply is not an indication of the truthfulness of their allegation.
It is up to the minister to state clearly his position in this regard. Why does he refuse to relieve the workers from their anxiety as to their future employment? They want to know if they will be unemployed tomorrow and if, like thousands of others, they will have to 21701-291
Montreal Postal Strike swell the already great number of unemployed in Canada, especially in Montreal and in the other areas of Quebec.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, if the Postmaster General was really serious and sincere, he would have asked immediately his colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) to act as a mediator in this conflict. Apparently, in view of the questions that we put to him recently, he would be ready to do it. The member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) asked recently the following question in the House: Is the minister ready to offer his services as a negotiator in this conflict? The minister replied then that he was ready to do so. Then, as a supplementary question I asked the minister if his services had been required. The Minister of Labour did not answer because we know as well as the ministers that the Postmaster General has not yet asked his colleague the Minister of Labour to intervene.
Why this silence, this indifference and this arrogance towards the working class? The workers are only asking for one thing: justice, the right to work and security of employment.
There are mechanisms which could be used. When I look at what is going on here, I wonder what is being done by the Minister' of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand)-and I regret that he is not in his seat-and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier), two men who, in days gone by, in the labour world, used to write-before they were elected to the house-that they were the great defenders of the working class, of the downtrodden, of the proletariat and of what you will. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, a former president of the C.N.T.U., should make a statement about this conflict and demand that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) come and solve it because he knows the mechanisms of negotiation well. He could certainly be a good adviser to the Postmaster General. In fact, those men who, in the past, achieved a reputation as great defenders of the workers are mute as fish. They do not say much.
We are confronted here with a serious conflict requiring immediate measures. We want and have to know what is the position of the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications and what he suggests to settle this dispute.
The minister has left us wondering whether the strike was illegal or not. It may be. He never gave us any information in this respect.

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike If the minister is aware of what he is saying, he will come and prove it to us but until then, may I tell him that under the contract binding the employees, 20 of them can stay away on union business without infringing their labour contract.
Mr. Speaker, we all deplore the vandalistic acts and the breaches of property which may have happened during this troubled period. Sometimes, we do understand the workers; we do not excuse them nor do we encourage them; we simply ask them to keep a cool head in spite of the minister's indifference. Still, Mr. Speaker, this conflict is a cause of friction, of anxiety and concern for those who only ask to make a decent living. The Postmaster General denies them this right, this inalienable right, the right to work which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) even wanted to entrench in the preamble of a new constitution.
I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, since my time is running out. Before resuming my seat, however, I want to be clear and practical. To get down to brass tacks, because we have to, I believe we still have a choice of six solutions.
First of all, the government could assume temporarily the responsibility for distributing the mail.
Secondly, the government could review the contracts now being negotiated so that the future employers will recognize the bargaining unit.
Thirdly, it could assure present workers that they will not lose their job at the end of March.
Fourthly, it could avoid unnecessary threats and provocations in official statements.
Fifthly, the minister could show a greater sense of justice and defend the right to work for everybody, as proclaimed by the Prime Minister when he talks about the establishment of a just society.
Sixthly, the minister should ask immediately his colleague, the Minister of Labour, to intervene in this conflict. In my opinion, the best solution is that the Postmaster General should simply resign, to every body's satisfaction.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief. I shall begin my comments with a couple of observations about the factual situation before I become involved in some areas of controversy. As I see it, the following are the facts.

There are now 459 drivers in the city of Montreal, employees of G. Lapalme Inc. and members of the CNTU, who are about to lose their jobs. In some cases these men have worked for up to 20 years in this employment. But as of March 31 they will be on the street.
How did this come about? It happened that the postal department decided for some reason, perhaps a good one, to split the region of Montreal into five new sectors in terms of the particular service these drivers were performing. As a result, instead of there being one contract for the work being done, tenders were sent out for five. It so happened that the firm for which these men worked did not submit a tender. The result, of course, is that there is no way these men can keep their jobs and 459 men, plus their wives and children, will suffer. I believe this fact should be kept very closely in mind.
The second fact is that the destruction of a trade union local is taking place. When we consider what the trade union movement has meant to the workers in this country and what it will mean to the future on our workers, we appreciate the significance of this fact. Perhaps the number is small in respect of the workers directly involved: it is only one trade union local; it is not a national trade union that is being squashed. However, in terms of the potential national consequences, I believe the significance of these facts transcends in importance the attitude of this government toward the working people.
It seems to me there are some very important questions which need to be answered by the minister. Why did not the postal authorities, for example, ensure that the jobs of these workers-these people who have worked for up to 20 years and who have been workers in good standing.-would be preserved even if a particular employer changed? Job preservation could have been made a condition of the calling of tenders; some effort could have been made to ensure it. But no report I have read has suggested, nor has any person to whom I have spoken about this matter, that any effort was made by the postal authorities to have these workers transferred to other firms if other firms were to end up doing the job.
Similarly, as was suggested by the hon. member who preceded me, why was an effort not made to ensure that the CNTU would still be recognized as the bargaining agent for these workers? This again, as has been indicated, could have been done by making
February 18, 1970

the CNTU, or one union local if you like, the bargaining agent for a number of firms. No precedent would have been set by this kind of action.
If it had been concerned about this question, the Post Office Department could have preserved the jobs of the workers involved for their well-being and that of their families. It could also have preserved an institution which is very important to these workers- the trade union local with which they had been associated. It seems to me that the opposite kinds of considerations have taken place, and it is hard to escape the conclusion that for whatever reason a deliberate attempt has been made to smash a trade union local. I think the minister has to answer for this action.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Quite beyond the particular question, it seems to me that this situation does suggest something about the government's attitude toward workers. How do they feel about the working people in this country, particularly about the people they employ themselves? A short while ago I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in this House whether he was considering taking action in terms of law which would make it mandatory for an employer to give substantial notice to an employee before releasing him from his work.
As is frequently the case, the Prime Minister said this was a provincial matter. For once the Prime Minister is absolutely right. Most areas of labour legislation are within provincial domain. However, there is one very important area which is not within the provincial domain; that is the area of federal employees. It seems to me the Prime Minister could have indicated at that time-as could the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) and other ministers of the Crown-in the administration of the government and its departments a humane and progressive attitude toward the working people of this country. The government has the constitutional authority to do that.
The federal government is in a position to be a pacesetter in terms of labour legislation and attitudes towards labour in this country. Instead, what do we get? There are some exceptions, but the general pattern of this government-and I must say it seems to be the general pattern of this minister-is to put all the emphasis on technocratic market efficiency at the expense, very often, of working people in this country.
Montreal Postal Strike
Again with particular reference to this minister, he is a man whose writings some time ago I admired because they suggested that at least here was one cabinet minister who knew something about modern social theory, who knew something about the nontechnocratic aspects of existence and who seemed, as my colleague suggests, to talk a good fight-at least prior to the leadership convention of the Liberal Party. Had I been a delegate at that convention I suspect I would have voted for the minister. However, I must say that his performance in office, to understate the case by about 100 per cent, has not entirely measured up to my expectations because he, of all ministers, has seemed to revel in a complete preoccupation with market efficiency. I suspect that somewhere at the heart of this dispute we will find this was the big question.
We will get this argument from the minister: We had to change our pocedures in Montreal. We had to change the employer that was doing the trucking because this would have resulted in a more efficient postal service. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that every serious, empirical study done in the United States and in Western Europe in the last ten years suggests that this kind of approach reaches the kind of conclusion we have here. It does not reach the conclusion that we have a more efficient enterprise, more productive and more contented workers. In fact we get just the opposite-discontent, inefficiency and wildcat strikes.
Every study in fact indicates-there have been a number in the past few years-that where working people are given serious consideration, where they are taken into the power structure in running enterprises, we get two very important by-products. We get greater, not less, efficiency by taking the worker more seriously. By treating him more as a human being we increase productivity. We also do this by giving him more power. All the evidence points to this fact.
The second and more important result so far as I am concerned is that you get happier workers, more contented human beings. I suggest to the minister that if he is really interested in efficiency he will begin to take the worker more seriously as a human being. Quite beyond that, I would like him to suggest to his colleagues in the cabinet, and particularly the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mack-asey), that the federal government begin to make basic changes in its management attitudes and in legislation as it affects federal employees. There is no better place to start

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike this kind of activity than in the postal service of this country, and no better time to adopt a change in attitude than during this current crisis in Montreal.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again we are faced with a Post Office problem. It is a pity, in a world where communications are increasingly important, that the department concerned is continually having this problem which, in fact, has never been thoroughly dealt with.
The department's policy is greatly to blame for the situation. All the solutions brought forward by the present Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kier-ans) have been superficial and short-term ones. The department is incapable of preparing a long-term policy. There is no dialogue, no regular contact with employees, no true spirit of conciliation and consultation. The minister's attitudes are always those of a dictator, designed to enforce his decisions. Such an attitude is ridiculous, when we remember the minister's assertion that increased postal rates would bring about an improved postal service. There is the record of this administration. It costs us more to get less service.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The minister pleads his case by saying that the conflict is illegal. Having said that, he stays put, he does not do anything, he does not try to meet-except at the very last minute-the union leaders.
Therefore, it is not surprising to find that the whole thing is a failure and that the dispute may reach the national level.
In the report issued by the firm of Kates, Peat and Marwich, the judgments were harsh. The minister remembers that. Indeed, as far as the public needs are concerned, as well as postal rates, manpower management, labour relations, working conditions, equipment, executive training, the report of this firm was particularly severe.
Unfortunately, this department has always developed a short-term policy. The Postmaster General, believe it or not, is the eighth minister in office since 1962. Thus, it is not surprising to note that, from one minister to the next, the policy is always a superficial and short-term one.
The least that we can ask from the Postmaster General is to prove that the recent rate increases are justified, due to the present situation. People are tired to bear the cost of strikes, even though they have no choice.
[Mr. Broadbent.l
When the communication phenomenon as a whole is affected, the situation goes much beyond the innocuous economic and administrative purpose.
We know that the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications has always been known for his letters. As this is precisely the question under discussion tonight I should like to refer you to the official report of the House for February 17, 1970. It contains a famous letter which will make him go down in history for his spirit of conciliation and dialogue. In fact, the minister in this letter describes his approach, that is that he has none.
This letter is dated February 17, 1970 and is addressed to Mr. Raymond Parent, Secretary-General of the Confederation of National Trade Unions. It reads as follows, and I quote:
Dear Mr. Parent:
Since the mail transportation situation in Montreal has become intolerable, I wish to state clearly the position of the Post Office Department and the Government.
Mr. Speaker, when the minister wrote those words, the dispute had already lasted for over 16 days, but that is not important. The minister finally made up his mind to speak, and you will note the conciliatory tone he uses, his ability in collective bargaining with regard to labour problems.
I quote further:
The resulting disruption, violence and intimidation have hampered enormously the competitive capacity of industry and commerce in Montreal.
Later on we find the following, and I quote:
I will not list the Incidents of violence, sabotage, and destruction of government property which have occurred during the last two weeks. You are as aware of them as I am. I will simply say that the mail is not being delivered.
Mr. Speaker, it will thus have taken 16 days for the minister to discover that the mail is not delivered, that violence occurs, and so on.
If you are looking for some indication of the employer's offer in the letter, you will not find any. Supposing that the employer, as such, recognizes that it is not the responsibility of the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications to settle the dispute, but of the contractor, one could wonder about the position taken by the Post Office and Communications Departments concerning the conflict.
February 18, 1970

The minister concluded his letter by stating three solutions, but nothing further was done. His first solution was as follows and I quote:
How can we assure the best service for the people of Montreal between now and March 31?
This first basic question asked by the minister in his letter is once again a short-term policy. He finds it essential to know how the mail will be delivered until March 31. He is not worried about giving an efficient postal service, but about what will happen between now and March 31.
However, the employees wish to know what will happen not only between now and March 31, but also after that date.
Here is the second question of the minister:
Secondly, how can we ensure the continued employment of the greatest number of present employees, with priority being given to the 162 men with more than five years service; thirdly, what are the best arrangements that can be made with Manpower to admit the remainder to paid retraining programs.
I eliminate the third one because the list of those who would like to benefit from the retraining programs is already very long. Let us examine the second question.
When I first read it, it seemed to have some merit. The means of ensuring job security at least to the 162 employees who had five years experience or more appeared to be worth considering. So I dug up the files and discovered something which I should like to bring to the minister's attention-a CNTU press release dated February 5, 1969. Obviously, the release was given to the newspapers and the minister and all members must have received a copy. I think it would be worthwhile to read it tonight, during this emergency debate. When I read it, I realized that I was right when I claimed that it was a short-term policy and that the second proposition of the government was unacceptable. The press release deals with the conflict with Rod Service Ltd. and reads as follows:
After that, the Post Office Department informed the union leaders that it would provide these services on its own, but it also called for tenders from three contractors, including Rod Service Ltd., in order to let out new contracts for these services.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we make a comparison, we find this is what is happening now in the dispute relating to Lapalme Inc.
The communique continues:
One thing is certain: the net result of all these operations is that 111 dismissals have been announced yesterday by the company to the union, 38 of which concerned the special delivery service and 12 the mobile delivery.
Montreal Postal Strike
During the dispute which took place in Montreal in August 1968, 111 dismissals were announced to the union. The union was caught off guard. They were ready for it in a way but not to the extent of fighting against a minister who disregards consultations and negotiations. You will remember the famous crisis of August 1968.
These same workers were then threatened to lose their jobs. They come up this year against the same problem. The quotation continues:
So, the wheel is beginning to turn:
-says the CNTU. And it was right because it had anticipated that the same release could be used again this year.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
On February 5th, the CNTU stated, and I quote:
-Ill employees lose their jobs, tomorrow others will also lose them. When will the 420 members of the union be out on the street?
That is the question the CNTU asked on February 5th in its press release; today we are up against the problem of knowing what to do with those employees.
Mr. Speaker, I should not overstay my leave but it seems to me that today's problem could have been foreseen. In spite of my limited experience in that field, it seems to me that if the Postmaster General had been more conciliating, had he worked harder at negotiations, if he had taken the trouble of going out to the parties instead of convening them to his office, had he gone out to meet the employees or at least the union leaders in short, had he taken into account the representations made in 1969, he might perhaps understand the drama now taking place in Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, it may be that government members will accuse us of wanting to play politics with this question, but by putting ourselves in the shoes of those employees who are threatened with being laid off, it is obvious to us that the department has a shortterm policy with regard to personnel management, personnel planning, and that the conflict could have been avoided.
That does not necessarily mean that the minister is solely to blame, but the fact remains that if the minister is honest, he will have to admit his failings, because he is mainly responsible for those lay-offs.
I suggest this conflict will increase more and more in scope in spite of the extraordinary measures the minister may take, espe-

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike cially if they are dictatorial measures, that do not rely on the co-operation of union leaders, on negotiation and consultation, and next year, we will have to cope with a new problem, even if the minister says it will not be next year, but five years from now.
It seems to me the communications field is of such importance that we should act seriously and try to prevent situations such as this one.
That we have known eight Postmasters General since 1962 seems to me significant enough. That is an indication that there is no long-term policy in that department, but a short-sighted one which may serve the ministers' interests while they hold office but surely does not serve the people's interests. Therefore, I invite the government members-without any political ambition but on the contrary very sincerely-to read the Kates, Peat and Marwick report and they will see that my criticisms are but a repetition of that report.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with rapt attention and great interest to the statement of the minister, which lasted longer than the rules for this type of debate allow. However, we were delighted to grant unanimous consent that he prolong his remarks and we on this side of the House will expect, if necessary, that similar reciprocation will come our way.
The minister spoke with great vigour and tremendous volume. He reminded me of one of my old elocution teachers who used to say that when you find your opponents roaring, you know that their argument is very, very weak. The minister used words like "bludgeon", "blackmail" and other brave words in talking about certain unions in Montreal and their iniquity. Since they were also asleep for five months, their iniquity must have been compounded during the few months that they were awake.
I used to read the telegrams and statements that union leaders addressed to or made about this present minister and often they came from the workers in his department. They made the most outlandish-as I then thought-denigrating remarks which I thought were excessive and extreme, and to which I was totally unsympathetic. After listening this evening to the outpourings of this minister, I can quite understand how the spokesmen for the unions feel. I can quite understand why he has been such a total disaster in the matter of dealing with the workers of his own department.
The matter we are discussing tonight on an urgent basis is not one that concerns only the people of the great city of Montreal. My colleague from Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) has discussed brilliantly and cogently the problems facing that great city. This is a matter that greatly concerns the whole country since the mail of many Canadians is processed in the metropolis of Montreal.
On the other hand, as a Canadian who is not from Montreal I want to say that I have no desire to see the people of that great city deprived of their essential services. The Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans), who spoke with such volume and apparent conviction as well as partisanship, is himself unique among the ministers of this unique government. In his short term of office he has emerged as an

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike outstanding curtailer of services and an eminent diminisher of jobs. Postmasters all over the country have found themselves sacked, their offices closed and the services that they have rendered to the people discontinued. People who have rendered faithful service over many more years than the minister has been in government have found themselves tossed out unceremoniously as the minister, with his technocratic sophistication, embarks upon making the Post Office pay regardless of the public and the needs of Canadian citizens.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Newspaper publishers, people who produce the non-profit press, who try to disseminate useful information for the Canadian people, long time users of the post office, have found themselves cast out because of this arrogant technocrat who was going to do such wonders for the postal service. He says the same things about the publishers as he says about the unions. He told us in committee that when the publishers said they could not publish under the new rates "they are selling you a bill of goods." He had the insufferable arrogance to tell me, "They are selling you a bill of goods, and you know it." The man who can presume to read the thoughts of other people is certainly no judicious interpreter of their actions.
In no area has this rapidly disillusioning government created more public resentment than in the Post Office, a department of government possibly closer to the average Canadian than any other. Many people will not be building new houses. Regrettably, many people are not tuned-in to external affairs and many people do not even pay income tax because they do not make enough money in these days of austerity. But most of us like to get some mail once in a while, and today we do not get it too promptly or too regularly. But tonight we discuss and we agonize over yet another grave deterioration in the postal service, one of the oldest and most essential utilities which the government of Canada owes to its people.
Since the present minister took office, what was bad has become worse and what was wrong has become intolerable. Tonight he had the presumption, which he has displayed before, to compare his record with that of preceding Conservative governments. I will follow him in that rhetorical exercise and say to him that he has certainly exceeded his Conservative predecessors and his Liberal predecessors also. He has exceeded both of

them because at no time since John A. Macdonald was postmaster has there been such dissatisfaction and such poor service as there has been since this technocratic expert assumed the office of Postmaster General. So if he wants to make comparisons, let him go ahead, but his record is greater than that of the Progressive Conservatives and greater than that of the Liberals-greater in ineptitude than both combined.
It is not surprising that there has been a shocking decline in the morale of the workers in his department. I have been here 13 years but I have been studying government for far longer than that. However, never have I seen workers in a department go to the public decrying what is going on in their department to the extent which has been the case in reference to the postal workers since this man took office. Those who want to read may refer to the press of yesterday or the telegrams of months ago from leaders of the unions in the Post Office Department to know what I mean. I have read into the record the statements of union spokesmen on these matters. As months go by we know that the mail accumulates and morale decays. That is the sad and dreary story of the Canadian Post Office in this the second year of the just society; this the second year of the announced satellite era.
Yesterday I read one of the most disturbing statements concerning a section of the public service of Canada which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen entitled "Death of Post Office Efficiency". It is a paid advertisement by the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada. I mention this because I think it is germane to the problem. I think we would be faulty in our analysis of this great public problem if we thought that the present discontent and the current troubles in Montreal were unique and isolated from the whole story of the pathetic, regrettable, constant and continual mismanagement of the Post Office Department. The paid advertisement to which I refer reads in part as follows:
The Letter Carriers of Canada wish to convey to the public, our deepest sympathy while they wait in frustration for mail they know should have arrived.
On February 17, 1969, a system called single mail processing was instituted in the Canada Post Office. This system was imposed full-blown by the minister to cut costs. In spite of this, figures recently published representing government estimates show that the Post Office will again operate at a deficit of close to $69 million for 1970-71.
February 18, 1970

They end up by saying, in a most unusual appeal from public servants:
We also ask you, the taxpayer, to contact your MP in an effort to have your dissatisfaction voiced in the House. Let us collectively bring back to the people of Canada the efficient postal service to which they are entitled.
It is signed, and presumably paid for, by the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada. I say again that this is a unique demonstration of relations between governmental employees and spokesmen for the government which, we can assume, is their employer.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
I thank the minister for his courtesy. This is what makes him such a success. His insufferable condescension has got him where he is. I would like to say, with all due respect, that I have read carefully the motion on which we are speaking. I listened carefully, without interrupting, although with a great deal of incredulity, to what the minister said. I am certain that what we are now discussing is part of the total decline in the morale of the employees of the postal department and I am wondering if the minister in his own remarks, or if anyone in the delineation of this debate, could properly suggest that we must confine ourselves

although I would be glad to do it-to the exchanges between those in Montreal and the minister himself. I am talking very definitely about the situation which is a grave one, so grave, so serious, so national in its importance that we are discussing it tonight under Standing Order 26.
It would be a partial and incomplete analysis to regard the Montreal episode as a separate instance. It is the last part of a regrettable story of abominable public relations and a pathetic failure to understand the aspirations
Montreal Postal Strike and priorities of the men whose work is necessary to make the department function properly.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The minister mentioned the appeal to the Minister of Labour. He waxed indignant about this. But it was not the members of this party who suggested the Minister of Labour be involved it was people involved more directly in the dealings of the minister who made this suggestion. I shall quote from a telegram:
The Confederation of National Trade Unions Wednesday asked Labour Minister Bryce Mackasey to intervene in Montreal's two-week-old mail delivery slow-down.
That is a euphemism, I may observe.
In a telegram to the minister, the CNTU said: "Our meeting yesterday, Tuesday, with Mr. Postmaster General Eric Kierans demonstrated his refusal to seek an equitable solution to Montreal's postal dispute.
We have received your public offer to intervene. That 450 workers are losing their rights concerns you in your capacity as labour minister and we ask you to intervene immediately to reach a solution.
So it is not from this party that the suggestion that the Minister of Labour appear as a saviour has emanated. It is from those others who have something less than confidence in the Postmaster General's ability that the suggestion has arisen. This situation, one of a series I regret to say, is deplorable. I think it is unfair to suggest that the whole responsibility resides upon those on the labour side, no matter how many years of seniority they may have. None of us has any right or reason to condone for a moment the violence which has been reported to us, but to heap scorn upon those on the other side-to use the kindest expression I can command-I submit, sir, is a most inadequate explanation of this regrettable and deplorable affair.
Some actions have been deplorable. I exonerate no one who meddles with the public's mail. Things have happened in Montreal which are beyond excuse. But I say in candour and sadness that the major blame must be placed, not upon the workers who have some reason to feel insecure but upon the minister whose record as an expert in labour relations has been deplorable when it has not been worse.
I think that instead of the superlatives of abuse which we hear about the excessive demands and actions of the union, we can never approach a solution, let alone an understanding of this acute problem in one of the

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike most important areas of the whole postal operation until we can invoke a little more objectivity, calmness and reasonableness. In all the discussions I have heard over this recent period, one which commends itself outstandingly to me in its objectivity and soundness is a statement made by a Mr. David Waters of the Montreal Star on the CBC the other day. Reflecting on this subject in a thoughtful way he said:
The drivers want job security, the Post Office wants to ensure efficient mail delivery, hopefully at a lower cost by contracting the delivery of mail through public tenders to independent firms. That it has proceeded to do by awarding contracts as of April 1st to five new Arms. The drivers claim that in the process their jobs and their futures have been jeopardized.
Then Mr. Waters asked:
How just is their claim?
He goes on, as a thoughtful man, to say:
Well put yourself in the driver's seat for a few moments and try to decide for yourself. Let's say you are 50 years old-
That strikes a chord because I am at the half-century mark.
-and have been driving a mail truck for some ten to twenty years. You are presently paid better than the average truck driver who works for some of the firms who have been awarded the contracts. You know that legally the successful bidders are under no obligation to hire you, to respect your seniority or any of the other provisions of the collective agreement which had been negotiated on your behalf with the company with whom you will be working until the end of March. You have heard it reported that Mr. Kierans himself intimated that the new firms may need only 350 of the 400 or 450 more drivers now employed. What has particularly galled you was the answer the Minister of Communications gave to your demands for job security. He suggested that if you ceased your protest-if you applied quickly to the new firms for jobs and if you asked the Manpower Department for help, he would be willing to help you in any way he could. In your view he meant if you are docile enough, if you apply cap in hand for a new job then men of good will at the top will do what they can for you-just trust them.

But should you trust them. If they cared about your future why wasn't fair treatment for you as to salary and seniority, etc., written into the public tenders put out by the post office. Most of the drivers have concluded that unless they protest vigorously by slowing down the delivery of mail their future well-being will most likely get lost in the shuffle. That distrust is not the fatality of dispute, but it certainly lies very much at the human heart of it. Meanwhile the undelivered mail piles up and the conflict grows more complex and uglier every day. By now everyone involved and that includes the public has become a victim of some kind of injustice. The mail must get through, the solution to the present conflict has to be found or one will have to be imposed. Whatever the outcome it will be wrong if legitimate insecurity of the drivers were not resolved in the process.
I noted very carefully the comment of the minister when he said the workers should take the risk of putting their names into the Canada Manpower office. Knowing how ineffective that particular branch has been in providing jobs, I can quite understand why he used that word.
Mr. Warren Allmand (Nolre-Dame-de-
Grace): Mr. Speaker, during the past two weeks the people in my constituency and the people in most of Montreal have been faced with a virtual breakdown in the postal service and with violence and destruction. These innocent, hard-working citizens of a city have been faced for a year with different types of violence and strikes. As usual, it is the innocent citizens who suffer, the old people who wait for their pension cheques, the small and big businessmen and people waiting for important supplies.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
As I said, the citizens of the city of Montreal during the last several months have experienced a wildcat police strike with accompanying violence, and a wildcat strike and violence among taxi drivers. They have been subjected to explosions and fires, destruction in their universities, violence in St. Leonard, and many other incidents.
Mr. Speaker, the sad consequence of much that has been going on and is now going on in Montreal is that these people who otherwise are very sympathetic to an open society, to democratic institutions, are demanding authoritarian institutions. I find this is an extreme and very disappointing side-effect of this whole situation.
As I say, the present postal situation is just another incident of many things that have happened in Montreal in the past year. I go
February 18, 1970

home to my constituency and face telephone calls, letters and meetings with people. They were moderate people, sympathetic to trade unionism and to many of the institutions of democratic society. But now they are questioning these things and wondering whether, if violence is the first principle of action by people who seem to have grievances, they must in protest demand authoritarian institutions. This is a real danger-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Order. For the benefit of the members of the House I will read the motion, which I have here only in English:
I ask leave, seconded by Mr. Valade, member for Sainte-Marie, to move the adjournment of the House under standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the postal
Montreal Postal Strike
slowdown in the city of Montreal which has crippled mail service, a concern which is within the administrative responsibility of the government of Canada and which has presently reached crisis proportions.

I feel that the statements of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace are relevant.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext: I do not agree with you.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
As a citizen of Montreal I am very much aware of the situation and I consider this debate important and serious. I am talking about the postal strike, the accompanying violence and the destruction of property that has gone with it. But I am trying to inform the House that one must look at this situation in context with all the other violence that has gone on in Montreal during the past year. I warn hon. members that it is becoming extremely serious when people, because of situations such as this, are beginning to question our democratic society and are demanding authoritarian institutions.
I find this situation extremely disturbing. I say that with all the sympathy that I have for the 450 workers who might lose their jobs, with all the sympathy for the points they may make in their favour and with all the sympathy I may have for trade unionism and the working people of Montreal, because Montreal is a working-class city. Even with all that sympathy, the people of Montreal cannot accept that the first principle of action in redressing a grievance or in trying to correct the abuses that may be against you, should be the illegal strike, violence and the destruction of property.
When the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) spoke he said, "let us speak about the facts." One very important fact he did not mention in this case is that the officials of this union, whose duty it is to protect the interests of the working men they represent, did nothing for five months. They knew this situation was going to arise. They did not take steps under the collective agreement to do the things they should have done to protect their workers. The first steps we saw in protest at the new situation were the slowdown, the violence and the destruction of property.
As I say, I am sympathetic to the situation of the men who are losing their jobs. I feel that it is unfortunate that matters have progressed to this stage. But I hope that even at

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike this stage of the dispute the unions and management, in this case the Post Office, can come together and work out a settlement for the good of everyone-for the good of the 450 truck drivers, for the good of the citizens of Montreal who are not getting their postal service and for the good of many others.
The purpose of this emergency dehate,, as I understand it-and indeed of all emergency debates-is that members of this House can contribute something to the solution of a problem. I think the minister has been doing his best in a very difficult situation. His emotions are taxed; he has been under great strain. Ever since he was appointed to this post he has been faced with lawful strikes and wildcat strikes. As he himself pointed out, of the last five strikes in Montreal only one has been legal and the other four illegal. If the procedure of emergency debate has any meaning, it is so that members of this House may contribute in a constructive way to the solution of a problem that constitutes an emergency. I hope that members on all sides of the House will do this.
I am going to put forward two suggestions. They are not original; they have appeared in the newspapers and have been put forward by other hon. members. I do not know everything the minister has tried but I hope that despite what he said he will still make an attempt to offer a guarantee of security to those truck drivers who have worked for a long time in the delivery of mail in Montreal. Perhaps he cannot do it for all of them.
As I say, I do not know how many attempts he has made already. I am sure he is well meaning. After all, it is certainly not in his interest to continue the strike. It would be very much in his interest to have this dispute settled so that he could go on to deal with other important problems. The minister is trying. He is taking great steps to improve the conditions of the workers in the central post office in Montreal. He is trying to put some of the recommendations of the Montpetit report into operation. But 1 hope that even at this stage of the dispute he will offer to guarantee work, at least to those drivers who have been trucking the mail for a considerable number of years.
My second suggestion is that the Department of Labour should lend a hand. I made this suggestion the other day in the House, but not as a criticism of the minister. I am not a member of the cabinet; I do not know how it works internally. But I am a supporter of the government and I feel when we have a

group of men who are experts, whose speciality is the settling of disputes, we should use them. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) has some top flight negotiators and mediators in his department. Perhaps it is time they were invited to help. Perhaps the minister has been too close to the problem. With all his good will and all his experience, perhaps he has come to a point where he just cannot deal with these men any longer. Maybe they cannot deal with him any longer because of the violence and the other harshness that has occurred in the dispute. So I recommend in all good faith that the Minister of Labour or the Department of Labour be invited to appoint a mediator or conciliator.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, it is a sad aspect of our society that because of violence, or where violence is used as the principle of action to redress a grievance or a demand, the majority of people in our society who are generally sympathetic to trade unions and to democratic procedures are now beginning to think in terms of authoritarian regimes to suppress violence.
I hope we will return to a civilized method of procedure, to negotiation, bargaining and mediation, and that through co-operation we will settle this dispute as quickly as possible.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister has mentioned in his speech tonight the atmosphere of violence which prevails in Montreal owing to the postal strike.
Previous speakers, including the minister himself, have given to understand that we did not propose this urgent debate because we favoured violence. Indeed we were wishing that the minister would expound clearly how he expects to settle the dispute, and how he intends to have regular mail deliveries in Montreal.
The hon. minister was very firm, which pleased the members of his party. I learned at the university that when a lawyer got angry and spoke very loudly in presenting his plea, it was because he had a poor case, and therefore we were advised to remain very composed because our colleague was on the point of making a mistake.
This is exactly what the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications (Mr. Kier-ans) has done tonight. He has offered no practical solution to settle the dispute.
February 18, 1970

He launched out at the CNTU, at the employees of G. Lapalme Ltd. and we are obliged to ask him to make a distinction. Not all Lapalme employees broke the law, only a small group. If the minister has any influence, he should ask G. Lapalme Ltd. to Are these trouble-makers.
What has been done until now? First, the minister demands that Lapalme employees return to work; then, accusations are made by the CNTU and the FTQ against the Postmaster General for his failure to propose a solution that would help these people solve their present conflict.
Last night, I watched TV when Mr. Laberge stated that the minister was incompetent, arrogant and aristocratic. Tonight, the minister has said in his speech that it was up to the government to decide, that he will not crawl on his knees before the unions and that the CNTU should face their responsibilities.
I therefore ask the minister how, in such an atmosphere of discussion, he can find a solution to this extremely urgent problem?

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext: May I reply to the question?

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE

speechtext: May I reply to the question?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, please tell me two minutes before my time is up that the minister wants to reply to my question.

speechtext:
We are in no
hurry.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
The hon. member is in no hurry? I hope he is going to make a speech as we have not heard him speak in the House for a long time.
I feel that the way the minister marshalled his arguments tonight will not improve the situation in Montreal.
Even though the minister accuses the CNTU, he must have only one objective, providing service for the population of Montreal and avoiding any disastrous economic consequences from the discontinuance of mail delivery in Montreal.
If there are any union problems, the minister will call upon competent people to solve them.
Tonight, the minister missed the boat! Had he proposed any solution, the situation would be entirely different.
If the hon. member on my right wants to make a speech, he can make it in due time,
Montreal Postal Strike but he should let me finish mine. It is not often that Liberal members from Quebec make speeches. We are anxious to hear them.
The minister did not say how he intended to settle the dispute. He concluded tonight, by saying that he wanted the dispute to drag on, suggesting that nobody would blackmail the government who is the master. The workers must be put in their place. The government must prevail. If the minister persists in this attitude for weeks and months, he will not improve the situation now existing in Montreal.
I am not for or against labour unions, but I am very concerned with human problems. The one we are considering now is the following: 450 employess of G. Lapalme Inc. have changed employer four times in five years.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Instead of trying to find customers to whom the trucks of G. Lapalme Inc. might be sold, as he said the other day in this House when he answered a question from the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), the minister should rather be concerned with the future of the 450 employees who are in danger of losing their jobs at the end of March. Mr. Speaker, there lies the real issue.
Even though the Liberal members from Montreal, headed by the minister, would like people to believe that this emergency debate was requested because we were glad there was violence in Montreal, I shall say to the minister that, like him, and like all other members from Montreal, we are against violence. However, we ask the minister to act in the interest of the people of Montreal and the 450 employees facing an intolerable situation.
The minister should be aware of the situation since it had already arisen with Rod Service Limited. He has decided to change the manner in which tenders are called and to divide between four or five districts mail delivery in the region of Montreal. But in four or five years, when these contracts expire, the minister will meet again with the same problem and will have to solve it.
Today he merely says that he cannot guarantee to the 450 employees that they will be rehired by the new contractors whose contract will come into force next April 1. What solution does the minister contemplate to help the 450 people who will be laid off? To go and register with the Department of Manpower and Immigration in order to get employment! And, as my colleague, the hon.

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) stated a moment ago, with our experience of that service, these people are not about to find a job in the Montreal area or elsewhere in Quebec, because that is where unemployment reaches its highest level, that is 8 per cent. And with a big smile the minister says: Personally, I can do nothing for the 450 employees who will be laid off on April 1 next.
Mr. Speaker, what is lacking in the Post Office Department's policy is planning. It was stated tonight, a short-sighted policy is applied, there is no control and, as one of my colleagues stated a short while ago, when the Letter Carriers' Union of Canada puts the minister's death notice in the papers when he is still living, that is a sure sign that the situation is worsening and that, obviously, the minister must do something about it. All my colleagues must have read in the newspapers the following notice:
In Memoriam. Efficiency of the Post Office Department.-February 17, 1969-February 17, 1970.
The Letter Carriers' Union of Canada was asking the population not to hold it against its members if the postal service was operating slowly, because the morale of Post Office employees was exceedingly low owing to the drastic steps taken by the minister since he became the head of that department. Indeed, he stated that he wanted to make the Post Office Department a profit-earning proposition, but for the years 1970-71, that department will still show a $69 million deficit.
These are figures and considerations on which it is well to ponder. I hope that the minister, at the end of this debate, will be allowed to say whether he will let the Montreal situation deteriorate or whether he has a practical and effective solution likely to settle the problem now existing in the metropolis.
There are some solutions. We are often told that the opposition can only complain and blame the government. Of course, our role is to criticize, though objectively; however, we must tell government members that we are not those who govern this country. The responsibility for taking the necessary decisions rests on the government itself. As far as we are concerned, we can help the government come to some decisions when it fails to find solutions to current problems, and in this case, when solutions must be found to the Montreal conflict.
How can the minister get out of this situation? Is he in a position to make arrangements through a negotiator? A Liberal

member who spoke earlier suggested the appointment of a negotiator who would intervene, in order to look fully into not only the problem of employees, but also that of an efficient mail delivery in Montreal.
I think that the first solution which the minister should consider would be to appoint a negotiator acceptable to all parties.
Secondly, what prevents the minister, if he wants to show some kindness, from urging those to whom the contracts will be given out as of April 1, to hire the greatest possible number of employees now working for G. Lapalme Inc. This is, in my opinion, the only efficient step which would show the employees of G. Lapalme Inc. that the minister wants to help them find solutions to their problems.
Besides, as long as Montreal and in the large centres of the country as well, we are not given a tender system imposed by statute, the minister will be faced with insurmountable difficulties.
When the minister rose to speak a few moments ago, I suggested, regarding the mail delivery and the postal system, that he set up a Crown agency that could award contracts to responsible companies which could hire workers on a permanent basis to ensure their continued employment. Those companies could provide supervision and a much more efficient planning than the present system. That is the only way out for the minister. A Crown agency could help in the planning of contract awarding and regular service, and could also bring job security to the workers.
* (10:20 p.m.)
The minister is now facing this problem in Montreal, but he will run into similar difficulties in Toronto, Winnipeg or anywhere else when contracts come up for renewal. I believe that the only way the minister could plan the policy of the Post Office Department would be to set up a Crown corporation with control over all aspects of the operation.
Since we are proposing objective solutions, the minister will not be able to claim that the opposition does nothing but criticize. We are not here to put the minister to the test but to help him get out of the mess he is in. If the minister were in our shoes this evening he would know just how many letters and telegrams we have received, not only from employees of G. Lapalme Ltd. but also from people who use postal services in Montreal
February 18, 1970

and others whose businesses are badly jeopardized because of that temporary interruption in the service.
As I said a while ago, we are not here to put the minister to the test but to help him. We are making suggestions to him and he should tell us, before the end of the debate, whether he accepts them and intends to deal humanly with the employees of G. Lapalme Ltd. in order to bring their problems to an end. In my opinion, that is the only way to cope with the situation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are holding an emergency debate this evening on the postal services and the problems now rampant in Montreal.
Of all members, I am perhaps most aware of postal services in Montreal. As Rod Services operated in my riding until last year, and the drivers for G. Lapalme Ltd., which operates further east in the city, used to hang around in a certain restaurant in my riding, and still do, I often have had the occasion to chat with them.
It is true that from time immemorial there has been a problem in that administration sector and that the present strike in Montreal, be it a slow-down strike or not-I will mention some facts to show that it is a deliberate one-is a source of serious trouble for the people. In fact, as the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) said a while ago, that strikes affect not only the poor who are waiting for cheques by mail but also the provincial economy and particularly that of the city of Montreal.
Last Monday, we did not get any mail in my office and last week we were two days without mail. That is the way it is in all business offices in the city of Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, this means that the economy suffers from that strike and that the CNTU leaders, instead of always blaming everything on the governments, the city of Montreal or public corporations, should assume their share of responsibility.
It is up to the minister and the government to provide the people with an adequate postal service.
But unions also have a responsibility as regards to the welfare of the employee and, in order to provide that welfare, one should not always rely upon governments.
It is also their responsibility to tackle the problem in order to solve it. While examining
Montreal Postal Strike the problem, we could compare the costs of this service in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
For the year 1969, when Rod Services Limited provided the mail service in Montreal, the cost to the Canadian government was $4.3 million.
Lapalme Inc. has a temporary contract. It was remitted to them when Rod Services Limited withdrew. They were told to take over mail delivery overnight. It will cost the Canadian people $5.2 million. With the five new contracts which were just signed by the Post Office Department and which will come into force on April 1st, it will cost $3.5 million. Therefore, there is a saving of $1.8 million.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext: Is it as efficient?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Charlevoix had his turn. Now he should listen to what others have to say, as he mentioned to other hon. members earlier.
Let us consider the cost involved in collecting parcels from mail boxes in two large cities of Canada where the cost of living is higher than in Montreal and in the Quebec province. In Toronto, it costs $20.75, in Vancouver $20.15 and in Montreal $25.60. As for colecting letters from mail-boxes it cost $6.11 in Toronto, $6.39 in Vancouver and $7.46 in in Montreal.
I have never heard anybody say that the employees were not paid enough. Their salary is $3.42 an hour but, as the minister said a moment ago, when the contract with Rod Services Ltd. expired, 397 drivers worked on mail delivery. But now, one year after the contract has expired, there are 455. Were the department to undertake the same work as that provided by G. Lapalme Ltd. they would have a payroll of 350, therefore 105 people fewer.
Surely, there is a failure somewhere. Why should we increase the personnel for the mere sake of providing them with jobs when it would be easy to find employment for these 100 people?
I am all in favour of unions, but not when they go beyond the limits of common sense. They sometimes go too far. In the Quebec province, however, there are a number of fields in which they would be welcome. Unfortunately, unions start growing where they thrive best. It is all too easy to say that the government should pay. But in the long run, who is the government? The government rep-

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike resents all the citizens of Canada. Were there no citizens there would be no government at all.
I often say to people that if the government has no money to pay, they go and get it in the pockets of taxpayers. Everything boils down to this. Now, the important thing is to restore the service in Montreal and to help the 300 or 400 drivers. I understand them, I know them. Several of them are married.
The minister said a while ago that 30 employees have been collecting the mail for 15 years and some for 43 years. About 162 of them have been doing this work for over five years. They practically have vested interests in their work.
The unions must also admit that they have no responsibility towards the department and that the department has no responsibility towards the unions. We may have a moral responsibility towards these employees, and I am sure that the minister offered his co-operation to the unions. The union concerned has even offered the minister to meet the members. Too often, in fact, when those strikes occur, three, four or five union leaders control the members and the whole association.
In proof of this, let me tell you that one of the new contractors whom I know ran an ad in the papers last week in Montreal, asking the drivers of G. Lapalme Inc. who were interested in joining his staff to apply to his offices, to make an application which would be taken into consideration.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
Until Saturday, no one had come to his office. Why? Because cars filled with goons and thugs were keeping watch over the entrance to his premises to make sure that Lapalme's drivers, CNTU members, would not apply for jobs. This is not logical. If the CNTU is so anxious to help the 300 or 400 drivers why did it not get in touch with the five new trucking businesses which will have the mail contracts from April 1 in order to help those people find a job?
Did not the 1969 contract linked with Lapalme stipulate that a six months' notice was to be given to the contractor as well as to the union before cancellation of the contract?
This notice was given in September by the Montreal postmaster.
It seems to me that, since September, the union has had time enough to foresee what was to happen to these drivers if it was that interested in their welfare.
As the minister said a moment ago, Rod Services Limited probably gave up their ser-
[Mr. Lolselle.l
vice in 1969 for the same reasons that led Lapalme Inc. to do the same, i.e. not to bid.
How is it possible for bidders to co-operate and to supply an appropriate service if they cannot, as we are told, hire or fire employees?
Unions are a good thing, provided that they do not go beyond the limits dictated by common sense. Unfortunately, in other fields where they should make their presence felt, they are not there.
It is the responsibility of the department to supply postal services to the people of Montreal and to the people of the whole country. However tonight we are concerned with the situation in Montreal. A short while ago, the minister gave the reasons for his attitude. Even if the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) stated earlier that he was not here to crucify the minister, I suggest that the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade) not only wanted to crucify him, but also to flog him beforehand. He called the minister all sorts of names.
On the other hand, the other previous speakers have dealt only with what they blame the minister for, which is normal. It is indeed normal to ask what is going on.
Hon. members should recognize that the minister gave a brilliant account of the present situation. He proved beyond any doubt that he was prepared to offer his co-operation, that he did offer it and that it was refused, because conditions were laid down to the department even though it has no obligation towards those people.
The department offered its assistance to help those drivers. They were offered the assistance of the Department of Manpower and Immigration and, as I mentioned earlier, it would be very easy for the union to negotiate with the five new contractors, so that they could hire those 300 or 400 employees. Why should the government assume responsibility for their hiring overnight? What will it do with those 400 men? Now that the new contracts have been agreed to, are we to impose a supplementary condition?
I believe that the CNTU leaders are not so stupid. They know that such a thing cannot be done. This would have been possible before, had it come to the minds of those concerned, on receiving their notice in September, that tenders would be called in November and that contracts would be concluded in January, taking effect on April 1. But no one worried about that. People would rather pay attention to other things, whereas those people should have been looked after.
February 18, 1970

I wish a solution were found, but there is no point in exasperating the government and blaming the minister and everybody, charging them with all imaginable sins, claiming that they do nothing and oppose existing projects; we shall not achieve co-operation in such a way.
The minister said a few minutes ago: We are prepared to enter into new negotiations to ensure better co-operation as soon as the illegal actions will cease in Montreal.
One of my friends told me yesterday that he had taken a certain street in Montreal and that he had followed a truck of G. Lapalme Inc.. I do not blame the contractor, but perhaps the driver. He had perhaps been forced by the union to act in a certain way.
But he was following the truck. Twice, the driver got out of his truck, bowed to the mail box, climbed back in and went away. That fellow was getting paid for his work but he did not do it.
Elsewhere, Monday morning, one of my Montreal employees advised me that on Park Avenue a mail box had been smashed and that the mail was scattered in the street. You are not going to tell me that such behaviour is not reprehensible. A while ago, the minister was blamed for his firmness, but I think that firmness is and will always be necessary. We want to help those people, but on the other hand, if they are paid to do that work, they are responsible to the department and the Montreal community for doing it properly.
The union has its responsibilities too. If it intends to oblige the employees to resort to violence to make the government treat them well, it is blackmail and the government should not yield to it.
A few moments ago, the minister said that some 500 mail boxes were ruined in Montreal and that some people had the "brilliant" idea of cementing the locks. And after such acts of vandalism, it is expected that the government will hire those people and will tell them: You were right, we shall give you certificates of good behaviour.
If a government did things like that, it would not deserve to be in power. If the minister ran his department in this way, he would not deserve to be Postmaster General.
I agree that these people should be protected, provided the drivers and the unions are also prepared to co-operate with the government. But the situation is not going to improve by leaving the people of Montreal to
Montreal Postal Strike
cope with such a problem. Undoubtedly, everyone has noticed that the worst problems of the Post Office have always come up in Montreal.
Even with the collective agreement, the situation has grown worse over the past two years. Again yesterday, I received a telegram from the Board of Trade telling me that conditions are unbearable. The employees should be left alone, the union should co-operate, the roughnecks, the bigwigs of the new employer should be thrown out. The new drivers should be allowed to find jobs.
The unfortunate feature of all such strikes is that while 500 or 600 union members are on strike they receive no pay whereas actually the strike was called by a few union leaders who control them and who continue receiving their salaries.
If, when a strike starts, the union leaders also were deprived of their salaries, strikes might be settled faster and more favourably.
But no. Baptiste, the little man, is on strike because the big wheels of the unions have decided to call a strike, to demand a raise of 30 or 40 cents an hour. But in the meantime, the worker does not get any pay.
Many strikes have been called in Montreal. One in particular, that affected a company on St. Patrick street, it lasted four months, after which the employees accepted the offer made to them at the beginning. The members of this union had been deprived of their salary during four months and it will take them two years to recover their losses.
The union leaders had not been affected by the strike. They lived quite well because they were well paid. Once they have settled a strike, they go somewhere else and start another strike. The unfortunate part of it is that the worker, who needs his salary from one day to the next, is always the loser.
He is not given a chance.
Actually, it seems that postal employees are prevented from applying to other contractors for employment. There are five new ones who will start operations in Montreal on April 1. Why not let the people who will be laid off be hired by these companies so that they can earn a decent living? Thus on April 1 they would start work for the new contractor. I wonder why the CNTU which is so interested in the welfare of these workers did not cooperate with these five contractors so that all the present postal employees may be hired again?

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike
Why blame the government and charge the minister with all the sins of the world? In fact, he has problems, he has responsibilities regarding the population and the union has some towards its members.
They should perhaps broaden theirs views, instead of always counting on the government. They themselves could perhaps try to obtain the means of helping their members from private enterprise and the public at large.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
Nobody can accuse the minister of having infringed the law or of having abused his rights. If he abused them, I think, it is by offering more than others.
The hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) said a while ago that there was some unrest, that the morale is low in the Post Office Department and that the situation looked bad. Under the Progressive Conservative government, federal employees were not allowed to strike.
Postal workers in Montreal had a hard time when the Conservatives were in office. They will tell you it was the worst time of all. We must not cover up the present sins with past sins.
As someone said a while ago the minister and the union have responsibilities to assume. The minister must act firmly but sensibly, and this is what he has done so far. This evening, he offered again his co-operation to the employees as well as to the union leaders. It is a question of wanting to co-operate. Let the union members co-operate also. Perfect strangers must not be allowed to attend the meetings. They should be actual members, and not people from outside who got their CNTU membership card as truck drivers only a week ago. Let us bring the members together with the minister. There exists a solution to the problem. It is not the end of the world but there must be some co-operation. Cooperation must not come only from the minister but from the others also.
