speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) said that the department

could be turned into a Crown corporation. I have already suggested it.
Even now there is a small area in Montreal where the department picks up the mail. I have not heard that there are any problems in that area. The problem might perhaps be solved, or at least 90 per cent of it, if a Crown corporation were set up. But before coming to that, other problems should be solved because, as the minister said a while ago, the problem exists across Canada. We should not have a small Crown corporation for Montreal, another one for Toronto, and yet another for Vancouver. There should be one single national corporation.
This is a human problem, one of equality and honesty for the citizens of Montreal. I trust there will be co-operation not only on the part of the minister but also on that of the union leaders and members, so that this situation may be solved in the best interest of the drivers, the members of that union, and also that the reputation of that association may be spared. The honour of the province of Quebec and of the City of Montreal must also be spared and their economy encouraged for it is now in sad shape.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the advantage this evening of listening to a very interesting debate and finding out a great deal more about the subject of torment to the largest metropolis in Canada. I was particularly interested in the remarks of the last speaker about the time when the Conservative Party had the honour of administering the postal service and how badly off the postal employees and the public were then. It seemed to us that our chief fault was that we delivered the mail on time and at a much lower cost than the present administration is able to do.
What kind of situation faces the people of Montreal? It is the people of Montreal with whom we are concerned and not the egotism of a minister or factors like that. We are concerned with public service and we have to find a solution to our problem. Having heard the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) speak in the chamber this evening, the main contributing factor to this difficulty obviously was laid bare in dramatic form. The minister was able to recount as well as his supporters incident after incident in this hot war between a union and the Post Office Department.
It is fine and good for the minister to take whatever advantage he feels he has in cloth-
February 18, 1970

ing himself in righteousness, pointing his finger at these incidents and saying that he will not be blackmailed. This would be a fine position if it were one that would work. But nothing the minister said convinces me that his position will work. The intransigence of the minister is at the heart of this problem, and the intransigence on his side is as solid and firm as it is on the union's side. There is a willingness to obstruct, to block to overturn mail boxes and to wave one's hand at mail boxes while going by.
So you have an irresistible force pressing against an immovable object. How does that solve anything for the people of Montreal? I think that the minister, who is a charming fellow in many ways, is about as flexible as a fossil. He cannot move. He takes his stand on a position and neither common sense nor the urgency that is so apparent in the city of Montreal can in the least way budge him from the position in which he finds himself.
The minister continually points to outrages with no suggestion of any action to cure them or the over-all situation. This simply leaves everyone floundering in the morass he and his party have created. When we consider the difficulties in the postal service over the last year and a half-and I shall stick to this particular problem-we find one common factor throughout the whole story: it is the intransigence of the Postmaster General. Once his mind is fixed on something, that is it. I do not think one solves any labour problem by being intransigent. One must have flexibility in his approach. I believe the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) in his question on Friday the 13th put it pretty neatly when he said:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Labour. In view of his success on the west coast and his other successes during the past year, would he consider offering the services of his department to the Postmaster General in settling the postal dispute in Montreal?
Hansard records some hon. members saying, "Oh, oh". I believe there were a great number of hon. members that day who said, "Hear, hear". Although Hansard records it as "Oh, oh", I think quite a number of us thought this would be one glimmer of light at the end of the rather long, dark tunnel into which the Postmaster General has led us. His pointing to these instances may warm the cockles of his conscience but it does not deliver the mail in Montreal. His somewhat facetious suggestion the other day that perhaps
Montreal Postal Strike the people in Montreal might stop writing drew its proper rebuke in an editorial in the Montreal Gazette.
We have the minister's intransigence on the one hand and on the other hand a feeling by the union people that there should be some security. We have had examples of people serving for as long as 43 years. If we cannot find a way to give security to people like this, we are in the wrong business.
No one on the other side of the House has been able to say that the rank and file of the union involved would not support their leaders. One can talk about harassment by goons and the like, but I have not heard any concrete evidence that this is taking place. Perhaps this is a Frankensteinian monster the minister is talking about. These people say they are going to stand and fight and that these things have carried on for a long period. This must be the case, if someone can give 43 years faithful service to the people of Canada. It would seem to me there is only one way to solve the impasse. It cannot be done in the posture which the Postmaster General adopted this evening. He should either turn the job of negotiating over to somebody else or the government should get rid of him. It is as simple as that. Obviously, he cannot solve the situation. Obviously, the longer he is there the worse the situation becomes.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the presence here tonight of all Liberal members from the island of Montreal and the area is surely an indication that the situation in which the people of Montreal now find themselves is of concern to all members of parliament.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Valade), who called for this emergency debate, did not see fit to stay in his seat to hear the retort. I believe the main dish that the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications, (Mr. Kierans) served him did not agree with him.
I think the minister might have thanked the hon. member for Sainte-Marie who gave him, through this emergency debate, the opportunity to really explain to the people the situation in which his department finds itself.
It is a serious problem, which deeply concerns not only the 450 employees of G. Lapalme Inc., but also the whole population of metropolitan Montreal. As member of this

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike
house, I felt duty bound also, even at this late hour, to take part in this emergency debate, tor a member's duty consists in keeping an eye on the interests of all his fellow-citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I will deal in my remarks with three different aspects of this problem: the economic aspect, the efficiency of the service as regards our fellow-citizens and employment security, which seems to cause great concern to the opposition members.
The population must be informed about the way the government considered those three aspects.
As was mentioned by the hon. member for Saint-Henri (Mr. Loiselle), from an economic viewpoint, we are going to save $1.7 million this year through public tenders and changes in the present system. This problem is urgent because this stoppage in the mail service is costing about $200,000 a day. And, what is even more important, losses in the business sector are said to amount to $1 million a day. That is why my first remarks deal with the economic aspect.
Now, mention was made of service and protection for the citizens. This is a point to be considered. In my opinion, there is not a single member who would go against the interest of the workers. But any rule goes just so far. We agree to protect the workers but we also want to know what that will cost.
Here I refer to the tenders called by the department on November 28 last. I think it was clearly indicated then that the tenderers should agree to pay salary rates at least equal to those in effect in the trucking industry on the day the tenders were called.
Furthermore, employment security was not for a year only but for five years. I think that the minister has really taken into consideration the security of the job for all drivers now employed by Lapalme Inc.
Now, to do justice to the G. Lapalme Inc. Company which did not tender for contract, which did not see fit to answer a letter written by Mr. Cormier, postmaster of Montreal dated September 25. May I say that here again, the question of employment security was considered. In fact, this is what Mr. Cormier had to say:
Your experience in local trucking and your knowledge of postal operations put you naturally in an excellent position to tender for a contract. We are expecting you to come forth with offers.
The Post Office Act provides now a five year period for transportation contracts. This longer period allows the successful tenderer to stabilize his activities in an efficient way as against the insecurity resulting from temporary agreement providing a one year term.

So when the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) blamed us for apparently waging war on the unions, this was sheer demagogy.
May I now be allowed to quote from an article in the February 5 issue of ha Presse, and written by Roger Champoux:
There is a limit to everything.
The Canadian Post Office has evidently scrupulously complied with the law. The agreement with G. Lapalme was temporary and the drivers concerned were surely aware of it. When the Lapalme company went out of business, the authorities had to look elsewhere, which they did. Who could blame them?
So I believe that all those points at issue which were raised were simply questions asked by the opposition members. Tonight, I think all their questions were really answered.
I now come to the following conclusions, Mr. Speaker. Tonight, we have seen in action a minister who has not always chosen the easy way out, but who has really assumed his responsibilities. He really called a spade a spade, and I think all the members of this house will want to support the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications who has looked fully into all the aspects of the problem and who did credit to his colleagues, as I said earlier, by not taking the easy way out and by facing his responsibilities as an administrator. He was easy-going, he examined the problems of the employees, the problems of the unions and the interest of the public and then came up with constructive suggestions.
When the interests of a country are threatened by a minority, the duty of the people's elected representatives is to protect the interests of all their fellow-citizens.
Those people, Mr. Speaker, show no regard for their own property as they have ransacked mail boxes which are public property. They have lost the respect of their colleagues, of their fellow citizens. I think they should be called back to order.
Mr. Speaker, the public is entitled to the service for which it pays. The government has a part to play, and the attitude of the hon. Postmaster General and Minister of Communications is really firm and positive.
From the information supplied by the hon. minister tonight, the situation has to be brought under control quickly so that the daily loss of $200,000 to the Post Office and of over $1 million to the business sector will be blotted out.
February 18, 1970

In my opinion, the department of Communications wants to help give a new impetus to the economy of Montreal which needs it very badly.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it only proper that I take part very briefly in this debate tonight, particularly in view of the fact that the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) may feel that the the wheat belt of Canada is not represented in this particular issue.
[DOT] (11:00 p.m.)
I remind the Postmaster General that what has happened in Montreal can happen elsewhere. We are all concerned about this matter. The point is that the Postmaster General should realize that you cannot use confrontation when dealing with people. Look at the newspaper headlines! One of them says, "Kierans warns CNTU to end postal tie-ups." I do not know whether the minister is warning the 455 people involved, or the entire CNTU. The newspaper article purports to report what the Postmaster General said yesterday. It says:
Postmaster General Eric Kierans said yesterday he will inform officers of the Confederation of National Trade Unions today that unless the Montreal postal situation returns to normal, the government will have 'no choice but to take extraordinary measures.'
Another headline says, "Kierans threatens quick move to cancel mail firm's contract". We heard tonight what a benign Postmaster General we have. It depends on your point of view: at times I wonder whether he is a sort of benign cobra. The Treasury Board has on occasion dealt with its employees as the Post Office Department appears to be dealing with its employees, that is, with a heavy hand. You cannot have collective bargaining with a heavy-fisted minister responsible for any department.
When the minister talks about extraordinary measures it means men will lose their seniority, the means of livelihood to which they have devoted their lives and jobs in which they have spent their whole working lives. It also means that there may be violence of the worst form; and that will destroy the minister's credibility. I think all will agree that you cannot run a Post Office Department as if it were a ticker-tape. Ticker-tapes have no heart or soul and do not consider the human consequences of any action. Ticker-tapes do not react to anything
Montreal Postal Strike in a human way; they only register money that is being put into and taken out of the stock market; and the money taken out, if a profit is shown, bears no capital gains tax.
People are devoting their lives to service in the Post Office. They are working for the people of this nation. They have hearts and souls and we must worry about them. One newspaper article says that the business community of Montreal and the people of the city have been suffering hardship because of the slow-down.
The Postmaster General ought to be worried about this situation. He should also be worried about people in other parts of the country who receive mail on only five days a week. That constitutes a slow-down. And who but the Postmaster General introduced it? He may laugh and jest, but he would not do so if he knew the names people all across this country are calling him. Some call him Eric the Terror; others, No Mail Eric; and still others, Heartless Eric. If I were not speaking in the House I might tell him other names that people call him.
If the minister were really concerned about the backbone service of the nation and about problems relating to mail delivery, distribution and handling, he would treat people as equals. This is no time to discriminate against a person because you do not like him. You may not like certain people, but you must treat them fairly. This is a basic human right that many people in government today are forgetting.
Let me also comment on the Postmaster General's suggestion that the present decision has the backing of the entire government. I suggest to the Postmaster General that if this decision does have the backing of all government departments, the cabinet must be responsible for the greatly reduced mail service in this country and the complete deterioration of the morale of people working in the Post Office Department because of the incredible attack made upon them.
We have heard the minister say tonight that there is a disruption of mail service to 2J million people at different times of the year. I suggest that the mail service has already been destroyed in so far as an effective system is concerned. At the same time the minister told us the union is destroying itself, driving employers out of business who are then asking to be relieved of their contracts. I suggest it would be pleasant to hear the other side of this story. I believe the minister is credible in many cases but too often we have

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike heavy-handed ministers who do not give us all the facts. In this situation we should hear both sides of the story if we are to know the whole story.
We have heard statements made by many people in responsible positions. As the minister said tonight, there are union leaders who are interested only in protecting themselves. Statements have been made on other occasions that people have deliberately tried to brainwash the public and lay the blame at the leadership level. I am not in a position to say whether the blame should be laid at the leadership level in this case. I have heard this familiar theme song many times. Until I have some facts to support that contention, I am not prepared to say that it is factual.
The greatest need today is for expert negotiations. I plead with the minister to ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) to send one of his crackpot negotiators-

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
-I mean one of the crackshot negotiators of his department to try to remedy the situation.
The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) made a few suggestions. One was the need for security for those displaced. We all agree with that. I hope when these people go to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) they will have the sympathetic hearing to which they are entitled. Another suggestion with which I agree 100 per cent is that we immediately assign one of the labour minister's negotiators to deal with this matter. I believe the minister should get away from the closeness of the situation. This was also suggested by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. The minister is too tense and worked up. Possibly this situation could then be resolved.
A member of the government should not come into this House, under any circumstances, and call people goons and other names and expect any labour organization or other association to have respect for him. We have heard in this House tonight people being called goons and other names. I ask the Postmaster General to put the record straight. When the minister talked about goons, was he referring to the CNTU as an entire body or as individuals; or was he talking about the 455 people who are worried about their livelihood? It is time the former leader of the CNTU, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), took a hand in

this situation. Let us see whether the CNTU is credible and whether the Postmaster General should be calling this organization the names that he called it tonight. If he was not calling the organization those names, to whom was he referring?
I believe the time has come for the minister to cease issuing press reports in the way he has been doing. We must not have confrontation in this situation. We must have negotiation if we want intelligent bargaining.
[DOT] (11:10 p.m.)

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not always agree with the policy of the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) but having listened carefully to his statement tonight, I must say that the position he took on the postal conflict in Montreal is in the interest of the people of Canada and particularly of the users of postal services in Montreal.
Since 1963, the Post Office Department established a complete reform programme of the postal service in Canada and the mechanism was set in action following the introduction of a report by the Royal Commission. A bill on management reform was submitted by the hon. Postmaster General and defeated by the Opposition. This modified bill has been again presented in October 1968 as bill C-116.
The purchasing of new equipment, the building of up-to-date plants and the increase in wages have entailled increased expenses for the Post Office department and bill C-116 was to correct partly this situation. Some members of Parliament, on the Treasury benches as in the opposition, have objected against certain clauses of this bill, and we have succeeded in amending it in the interest of all the users of postal facilities in Canada.
From an article published by La Presse in October 1968, I quote the following excerpt:
The most active defenders of Mr. Kierans' bill are the postmen themselves.
For Instance, yesterday, when members of the opposition parties continued to harass Mr. Kierans in the House of Commons, the president of the Canadian Postal Unions of Canada, Mr. William Houle, declared that the postmen had been fighting for 10 years for such a reform in the Post Office Department. In fact, Mr. Houle has indicated in an interview that the way things are run today in the postal services has been a major cause of the two strikes of the employees in the last years. According to Mr. Houle, the posties are backing unreservedly the bill in its present form. He added that concession appeared acceptable, that of leaving post offices open in rural areas, that is where this would not give to any or very little additional costs.
February 18, 1970

He is interested in expenditures. In this act, to which Mr. Houle gives his wholehearted support, section 22 reads as follows:
Before entering into a contract for the conveyance of mail involving an annual expenditure of more than one thousand dollars, the Postmaster General shall, for a period of at least three weeks, display public notices inviting tenders for the contract in post offices and other public places within the area to be affected by the contract and may, by any means, give such other public notice of the invitation to tender for the contract as he considers desirable.
And subsection (2) reads as follows:
Where mail is conveyed pursuant to a contract referred to in subsection (1), the Postmaster General, if he is of the opinion that it is in the public interest so to do, may with the approval of the Governor in Council discontinue the conveyance of mail pursuant to such a contract and instead cause it to be conveyed by postal employees in vehicles owned or leased by Her Majesty-
When the president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, on behalf of all its members, was in agreement with the proposed bill, namely Bill C-116, he was also in agreement with section 5. The procedure followed by the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications is consistent with the act passed by Parliament on October 28, 1968.
Again pursuant to the act, the department made it known on September 26, 1969, that tenders for contracts would be made for the transportation of mail by truck in Montreal.
As my colleague from Montreal has indicated, a zoning service was tried in the Montreal east end in 1966; it produced a better service and allowed the department to achieve a more efficient control. The experiment was carried on and, after a few years, the Canadian Post Office decided to split the Greater Montreal service into various zones. That did not happen unkown to the labour unions. Everybody was aware of the decision, as well as of the temporary agreement that was concluded with G. Lapalme Inc., pursuant to Section 5 (2) of the act. The agreement's duration was of one year only and again the union was aware of the terms involved.
The minister's responsibility is to enforce a legislation voted by Parliament. If the minister had not let the live contracts according to the stipulations of the act, the opposition, which today requested an urgent debate, would have been first to criticize him and to call him to account, to ask explanations. He would have been asked why he had not enforced the legislation to which, as I said earlier, Mr. William Houle, president of the
Montreal Postal Strike post-office workers of the Canadian Postal Unions, had given his complete approval in 1968.
The conditions have become entirely unbearable for the Montreal population and the effect of the delayed mail delivery in Montreal is felt throughout Canada. The statistics provided by the minister on postal services in Montreal show that they are more costly than any other similar services in other large Canadian cities.
Under the new contracts, the Post Office and Department of Communications, that is the Canadian people, will save $1,100,000. This is a clear indication that this government agency wishes to operate as efficiently as the best-run big businesses of the country.
I agree with the minister who invited the union members to take advantage of the opportunity that is offered to them and apply for jobs with the new contractors.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just listened to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) explain the situation as he sees it. Among the things he suggested was that the situation has become untenable for the people of Montreal. A Liberal backbencher earlier in the debate said that he wished to call a spade a spade, and I agree with him in that regard.
[DOT] (11:20 p.m.)
I agree with the hon. member for Gaspe because I believe the situation in the Post Office Department has not only become untenable for the people of Montreal but it has become untenable for the people of Canada. The main reason for this situation is the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kierans). I do not think there is any doubt that if the Minister of Communications or any of his public relations people were to go across the country and ask the people of Canada who was the best-known individual in the Trudeau government, some might not know who Mr. Trudeau is but all would know who the Minister of Communications is.
They might have something else to say; they might say that he is the most disliked man to ever hold a portfolio in the history of this country. That is as it should be, for since this government was elected on June 25, 1968, there has been a catalogue of failures so far as public relations in the Post Office Department are concerned. Time after time this House is faced with a crisis because the Min-

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike ister of Communications has foot-and-mouth disease. There are times when he cannot even take the time to take one foot out and put the other in.
This situation is a sad commentary on the government, the more so because it will not get better. I believe that the greatest thing that can happen to the people of Canada is to have the Post Office Department made a Crown corporation, because by doing that they will get rid of the Minister of Communications. That would be a grand day for everybody in this country, and for good reason. Here we have a situation wherein negotiations are supposed to be going on with the employees, and we have the minister suggesting that he will find 350 unemployed people to take the place of those who have held positions for many years and felt they had job security until the minister opened his big, fat mouth again and put his foot in it.
Here we are on Wednesday evening at 11.25 p.m. talking about the Post Office Department, when if almost anyone else held the portfolio in question we would not have to be here because the crisis would not be upon us. It is a sad situation for the people of Montreal. It is a sad situation for the people in my constituency, especially my rural constituents who have witnessed the closing down of 25 post offices, the elimination of service after service that has always been available to them and having reduced service at greater cost. Everything that you would imagine a government would not do, this government has done. Why? Because this minister who comes from the city of Montreal has no appreciation or understanding of what it is like to live in a rural community. Apparently he has no appreciation of what it takes to run a business in this country and what is even worse, apparently he does not care.
This government has been referred to as a plastic government, a government without heart, a government without blood in its veins. Never was there a better example of that type of administration than in the performance of the Minister of Communications. He cares not one iota for the problems of the people in the rural communities of this country. He apparently cares not very much more for the business community in this nation, because he allows unthinkable things to happen within his department. Instead of correcting the situation and allowing his negotiators to try and solve the situation, he makes public utterances on behalf of himself and no one else which make it impossible for the negotiators to do their job.

I can think of nothing worse than to be a negotiator involved in postal matters in the Department of Communications working under the present minister. It is a wonder he has any negotiators left. I just shake my head every time I go home, because my constituents come up to me one after another complaining about this, that and something else concerning the Post Office Department. The minister tells us the same thing every time; he tells us he is saving money.

speechtext:
It is bad the way you do it, my
friend; it is mighty bad. I will tell you something else. If the Minister of Communications would ask the people of Canada what should be done, they would say, "Put the Post Office back the way you found it in 1968, and we will gladly pay the extra money because we will have some services once again."

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext: You do not mean 1968; you mean 1868.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
The minister says I mean 1868. I tell the minister he can set up all the Liberal backbenchers he likes and they can read ad infinitum in extolling his virtues; and when they are all through, the sum total of the improvement they will make to his public image will be a big, fat zero-because he is dead; he is as dead as any man has ever been in the history of Canada so far as politics are concerned. I am not quite certain about that, because the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Lang) is matching him or running a close second, especially after his performance on Tuesday afternoon.
Never in the history of Canada has such a catalogue of failures in such a short period of time been placed before the House of Commons for consideration as we have had in respect of this minister. He is in hot water all the time. One would think the minister when shaving in the morning would stop, take a good look at himself and say, "Maybe somebody in Canada besides me is right. Maybe I should stop and think for a minute and consider whether all these situations in which I am embroiled are not my own doing." Perhaps he should say to himself that he is partly wrong.
If he did that, it would be a big step in the right direction and perhaps we would not be sitting here quite so often on Wednesday nights debating postal matters, talking to the minister and trying to make him aware that everybody does not live in a penthouse in the
February 18, 1970

sky which no one can reach, where no one can tell him anything or negotiate with him. Everybody in Canada receives a miserable service from a minister who gives a miserable performance and who should resign for the good of the country. This would be the greatest thing that ever happened to Canada.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE MONTREAL POSTAL DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a moment ago when I heard the member for Saint-Henri (Mr. Loiselle) say that people cannot breathe or live in Montreal any more, I fully agreed With him. It is probably because they vote for the Liberal party.
Later, I heard the member for Laval (Mr. Roy) say that all the members from the Island of Montreal were present this evening. I counted exactly three of them. Either the member for Laval cannot count, or he wants to make fun of postal employees. We all know that the member for Laval often laughs at farmers, but I hope he will not go so far as making fun of postal employees.
We have before the House today a motion of censure involving the Post Office and Communications Department. I would like above all tonight-as it will soon be midnight-to explain why such an explosive situation prevails in Montreal.
The department and the minister have tonight been accused of all the world's sins. It is true that the minister may suffer from political far-sightedness particularly when he states that we have only up to 1975 to bring order to the Post Office.
Perhaps he feels more comfortable in the Department of Communications from where he can better contemplate the vast spaces and dream of glamorous projects to be realized around the year 2,000. However, he should be more realistic and prove that he has his feet on the ground by settling the problems cropping up in 1970.
[DOT] (11:30 p.m.)
Thanks to him, since the revision of the postal rates, several newspapers and magazines which made it possible to bring culture to all the regions of the country have folded, and that has caused dissatisfaction throughout Canada.
Today, the labour union are aware of this problem. These magazines reached the people before the revision of the postal rates at a fair price and allowed some degree of culture to reach all the regions of the country. By
Montreal Postal Strike wanting to put his department on a profitearning basis, the minister is, on the contrary, accumulating a deficit which is said to be this year of the order of $70 million. Thus, the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications is automatically responsible for that dissatisfaction and for the very explosive situation that prevails in the Montreal region.
However, I suspect that several of his Liberal friends, who want his head, led him to believe that it might be possible to get the Post Office and Communications Department to pay its way, knowing that it will be difficult for him to get out of this tight spot.
And, as though to rejoice about his attitude, they advised him to increase rates, a move designed to make him so unpopular with the population that he would be forced to resign.
I must admit that the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications has had the courage to do away with patronage, particularly in rural and semi-rural communities. Small town post offices, for example, and contracts awarded for rural mail delivery are not subject to patronage as they used to be.
At least, he has this to his credit, and we hope that he has not done away with this patronage, only to replace it by another less palatable one, as we see now in Montreal, by wanting to divide up contracts in four and, possibly reduce the efficiency of the Union representing the postal employees. By reducing the Union's power, he is fueling the explosive anger that we are now experiencing.
On the other hand, a company that has submitted a tender under a fictitious name, in Montreal, leaves us nonplussed. I hope the minister will not let this patronage practice that we meet far too often, take root in Montreal.
In the field of postal service, priority should be given to the immediate needs. It is not by pretending to ignore the problems and trying to find patched-up solutions that we shall solve the problem on a permanent basis.
Besides, relying on attrition to settle a question is not a viable formula. Instead of letting his mind run upon satellites and computers and of dreaming of making his postal empire competitive with the big telecommunication corporations, the Minister should do his utmost to solve the pressing problem of mail delivery, which is appalling everywhere totally non-existent in Montreal.
The hon. Minister wanted to simplify a problem which seemed unsolvable and try an

February 18, 1970
Montreal Postal Strike accounting type of approach. He first decided to raise postal rates. Then, he did away with mail delivery on Saturday. Then, as a next step, he denied to a great number of publications the privilege to remain in the category to which they ought to belong, thus raising a general outcry. As for us, from the Rallie-ment Creditiste, we had at that time, warned the hon. Minister against his mistakes. I have here a statement from the Committee of fair postal rates and if union representatives are not satisfied with the administration of the Postmaster General and Minister of Communications, I would say that they are not the only ones in Montreal. Also, among others, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Society of Public Welfare, the Union CoOperative of Canada, grouping ten other organizations, which are the Canadian Association of Home Economics, the Canadian Consumers Association, the Canadian Association of Industrial Editors, the Canadian Association of Social Workers, the Indian and Eskimo Association, the Canadian Council of Urban and Regional Research, the Canadian Federation of Professional Women's Clubs, the Canadian Federation of Teachers, the Chemistry Institute of Canada and the Scouts of Canada have expressed their dissatisfaction to the minister. The responsibility for the explosive conflict in Montreal is not that of the unions alone since all the organizations that I have just mentioned had warned the Minister that the situation was deteriorating.
What had they recommended to correct the situation that we are now experiencing and to stop the criticism to which the Minister is subjected? First of all, they had asked that third class rates applicable to organization publications be brought back to the level of the second class commercial publication rates. As the Minister claims that commercial publications are now paying their fair share, there
is apparently no justification for charging higher rates to organization publications when the handling of such mail is the same in both cases. They had then asked that the periodicals of associations be considered as a separate group within the third class mail.
Finally they wished that the present rate classification of 10,000 emits for bulk delivery be lowered further to the same level as before, with regard to the rules for third class mail. Since the minister refused to comply with those requests, he caused dissatisfaction throughout Canada. All those organizations are almost happy to witness this explosive situation and the minister does not get any sympathy. Seeing he refuses to admit all those facts, there is only one thing left for the minister to do. He should have the courage to do what the ex-Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) did and resign from his post.
His refusal to admit his mistake has created an intolerable and disastrous situation which, to my mind, can become very dangerous because of the abuses it could lead to from both sides.
Finally, as several of his colleages and so-called liberal friends want his hide at all cost, because his good friend Rene Levesque, former member of the liberal party, does not protect him, he should like the former Quebec Minister of Justice and the former Minister of Transport, resign from his post in order to be able to leave the liberal party with dignity and say: "I leave happy."
